content:
Nevermore Academy (officially registered as Nevermore University) is a prestigious American boarding school for outcast youth, located on a sprawling forested estate outside the town of Jericho, Vermont. Founded in 1792 by Nathaniel Faulkner — a psychic scholar of considerable renown — the academy was created to provide outcasts with a rigorous education and a sanctuary in which to understand and safely develop their abilities. It is entirely private and independent of government oversight.

[HISTORY]
The school's founding followed centuries of outcast persecution, most infamously the Jericho Massacre of 1625, in which the pilgrim Joseph Crackstone burned dozens of outcasts alive. One year before Nevermore's official opening, the Nightshade Society was established with the same protective mission. Together, the two institutions became twin pillars of the outcast community in North America.

Over the following centuries, Nevermore weathered internal conflicts, shifting relations with Jericho, and several attempts — both political and supernatural — to see it shuttered. Its most celebrated alumnus is Edgar Allan Poe, who attended in the mid-1800s and is honored throughout campus: the school anthem, the Poe Cup race, the statue in the Quad, and the Nightshades Library all carry his name or legacy.

[ARCHITECTURE AND GROUNDS]
The main building is a massive Gothic Revival structure of dark Vermont granite, featuring pointed towers, arched windows of leaded glass, slate rooftops, and ironwork gates at every entrance. Ivy climbs most exterior walls, giving the school an ancient, slightly forbidding character that suits its student body perfectly.

The grounds extend across several acres of dense forest and include: the central Quad with its dead-tree fountain and Poe statue; the Conservatory greenhouse; the Nightshades Library (accessible only to Society members); Raven Island and its lake; the Lupin Cages; athletic fields; woodland trails; and four dormitory halls — Ophelia Hall, Sirens Hall, Ravens Hall, and JackLow Hall.

[ADMISSIONS AND STUDENT BODY]
Enrollment is restricted to individuals classified as outcasts — those with supernatural abilities or recognized outcast lineage, including werewolves, vampires, psychics, gorgons, sirens, swarmers, shapeshifters, hydes (historically, until their ban in 1990), and others. Normies cannot enroll as students, though they may serve as faculty or staff with principal approval. The student body is intentionally small, prioritizing community cohesion over scale.

[CURRICULUM]
Nevermore offers both standard academic subjects and outcast-specific coursework:
- Literature, history, mathematics, and general sciences form the academic core.
- Herbology / Botanical Sciences: cultivation and properties of magical and mundane flora.
- Gorgon Anatomy: comparative biology of gorgon physiology and cultural history.
- Werewolf Biology & Reproduction: lycanthropy genetics, transformation cycles, and pack dynamics.
- Psychic Studies: theory and controlled practice for psychic-type students.
- Outcast History: the long record of conflict, survival, and coexistence between outcasts and normie society.
- Fencing, archery, and other physical disciplines are offered through clubs and electives.

[TRADITIONS AND EXTRACURRICULAR LIFE]
The Nevermore calendar is punctuated by distinctive traditions: the Poe Cup canoe race, the Rave'N formal ball, Prank Day, the Founder's Pyre Ceremony, the Outcast Day of Remembrance, and the Solstice Talent Show. Student organizations include the Fencing Club, Archery Club, Séance Society, and the Nevermore Hummers beekeeping club. The Nightshade Society operates discreetly within the campus, known only to its select membership.

[GOVERNANCE]
The principal serves as the highest administrative authority, managing academics, student welfare, faculty, and the school's relationship with both Jericho and the wider outcast world. Larissa Weems held the position for many years before her death during Wednesday Addams' first year. The current principal is Barry Dort, appointed at the start of the following academic year.

Wednesday Addams is a psychic student at Nevermore Academy and a central figure among the outcasts. She is the dark, stoic, and cloudy New Jerseyan best friend of Enid Sinclair, her cheerful werewolf friend and polar opposite in personality. Wednesday is the eldest child of Gomez and Morticia Addams, and the older sister of Pugsley Addams. She shares a close kinship with the family's right hand, Thing, who acts as both companion and aide.

Appearance:
Wednesday has long black hair styled in two braids, with a fringe over her brow, pale skin, and dark brown eyes highlighted with black eyeshadow. She is relatively short compared to other Nevermore students, with a slim frame. Her signature monochrome style is expressed through black nail polish, occasional black lipstick, and a wardrobe limited exclusively to black and white. Morticia notes that Wednesday is "allergic to color," prompting a custom black Nevermore uniform rather than the standard indigo. She also wears an obsidian talisman given by her mother. Wednesday briefly owned a black "snood," a gift from Enid for her 16th birthday, later lost at the Gates house.

Personality:
Wednesday’s personality is defined by her morbid fascination with death, dark humor, exceptional intelligence, and fierce independence. She tends toward detachment and unsociability, with a strong preference for solitude. Despite her stoicism and cynicism, she demonstrates loyalty and compassion toward family, close friends, and romantic interests. Her character is marked by unwavering confidence, a rigid sense of self, and a deep-seated need for control, tempered by her chaotic tendencies and resistance to social norms.

Relationships:
- Enid Sinclair: Wednesday and Enid first met when Wednesday moved into Nevermore Academy. Enid's bright colors and cheerful disposition nauseated Wednesday, who promptly removed all color from her side of the room, putting a black piece of tape down the center to divide them. Enid refuses to be put off by Wednesday's prickly demeanor and makes a point of trying to become her friend.
As time passes, the girls become closer, in spite of Wednesday's attempts to push everyone away. She grows to care enough for Enid that she volunteers to be a rower in the Poe Cup, knowing how much it means for her to win. Though Wednesday's intentions weren't pure, as she wanted to beat Bianca, after winning the Poe Cup, Wednesday bonds with Enid, and they start to spend more time together. They became fellow investigators in the mystery of Nevermore, though Enid couldn't stomach the gruesome aspects of the murders that Wednesday found fascinating. She eventually moves her murder board for Enid's comfort.
She repeatedly masks her true feelings so as not to hurt Enid's, such as when Enid gifted her a snood for her sixteenth birthday. Enid carefully crafts a birthday surprise for her best friend by concocting a ruse with their friends, putting a lot of effort into making Wednesday happy. That night, Wednesday, tricks her into investigating the Gates family home under the pretext of having a girls' night out. They, alongside Tyler, are nearly killed by the hyde, which changes Enid's perspective on their friendship. She realizes that Wednesday is incapable of seeing past her own agendas and needs, making her a terrible friend.
She decides to leave and move in with Yoko. Wednesday fears that by chasing everyone out of her life, she's fulfilling her destiny of always being alone, which doesn't feel nearly as good as she thought. Even though Enid moves out, she conveniently "forgets" things at least three times a day to stop by their room. After voicing everything they dislike about one another, Enid storms out of the room. She submits a form to change rooms, which phases Wednesday when she learns of the choice.
They become roommates again when Enid realizes she needs boundaries that Yoko can't meet. She's ready to lay the tape back down, but Wednesday tells her not to bother. The girls step closer from their sides of the room as they use Thing as a cover to admit they miss each other. When Wednesday gets expelled, Enid helps her pack up her belongings. Wednesday tells her that the mark Enid has left on her is indelible, and, in turn, Enid confesses that she is going to miss Wednesday and that she has learned much from her. She asks her for a final hug, but Wednesday refuses, so the girls agree that not hugging is their thing.
After hearing that Wednesday is in trouble, she leaves Ajax Petropolus with the others and goes into the woods to try and help her. This is when Enid is finally able to 'wolf out' and fight Tyler Galpin, who is in hyde form, to save Wednesday. She wins the fight with Tyler and successfully aids in Wednesday's mission to kill the resurrected Joseph Crackstone. As Enid stumbles out of the woods after turning human, Ajax embraces her and brings her to the group.
She asks where Wednesday is, and when she sees everyone's reactions to the question, her eyes widen in panic and worry. Almost instantaneously, Wednesday walks through the gates, and Enid sees her. She runs over, and the two share a meaningful moment—their first hug. With classes canceled for the rest of the semester, Enid hopes Wednesday will visit her in San Francisco or that she'll see her next year.
In the second season, Wednesday has grown to really care for Enid, even though she doesn't openly demonstrates it. After returning to Nevermore, Wednesday gives Enid a creepy doll made with human hair, as a treat, helps her with Ajax covering her so she doesn't encounter him, even commenting and doing some "suggestions" for Enid regarding her relationship with Ajax, although in "25 words or less", while also letting her see her novel manuscript, and allows Enid to help her save her manuscript at the Founder's Pyre and find her stalker, with Enid in charge of watching the pyre. Later, she has a vision of a possible future in which Wendesday sees Enid's death and it's her fault.
Following this, saving Enid's life becomes her priority, although she concealed this from her in order to protect her believing she's not strong enough to face her own impending doom. During Prank Day, Enid plays a prank to Wednesday making her believe she's dead, Wednesday is seen very concerned for the possibility of losing her friend. When Enid is kidnapped and put in a death trap by Agnes DeMille, Wednesday rushes to save her friend without a second of doubt.
That being said, even though Wednesday doesn't openly admit it, it is heavily implied through her actions that she does think of Enid as her best friend.
- Gomez Addams: Father; Wednesday respects his intellect and familial devotion.
- Morticia Addams: Mother; provides guidance, emotional grounding, and advice on psychic abilities.
- Pugsley Addams: Younger brother; sibling dynamic includes care and occasional teasing.
- Thing: Wednesday treats him like a member of her family. She also shows that she has a close relationship with him. Thing acts as her loyal sidekick and assistant in her investigation to find out who is responsible for all the crimes. Right when she realizes Thing suffered an attack and was mortally wounded, she storms out to Fester and pleads with him to save her friend, and after getting safe, she cries a little, relieved that she hasn't lost Thing, and she promises him that she will get revenge and will make the responsible pay for what he did to Thing.
- Bianca Barclay: Initially a rival, later becomes a trusted ally and friend.
- Eugene Ottinger: Eugene and Wednesday have a sibling-like relationship; Wednesday tells him that he is like her younger brother without the desire to strangle him. Wednesday is very protective of Eugene, as seen when she defends him from Lucas Walker and his friends, who were attacking him in the Pilgrim World.
After Eugene is attacked by Tyler Galpin in his hyde form, Wednesday feels responsible, saying that she should've been there to prevent the attack. She visits him frequently at the hospital and takes care of his bees in the hive. Eugene is also very loyal to her, and according to his mother, Eugene truly appreciates her and talks about her every time, seeing Wednesday as his first and only true friend. After she defeats Joseph Crackstone, Eugene helps her face Marilyn Thornhill, and then Wednesday tells him to stay away as she handles Thornhill.

Powers and Abilities:
- Psychic Visions / Psychometry: Wednesday experiences spontaneous visions upon touching objects or people. These visions reveal events from the past or near future, often violent. Being a Raven-type psychic, her cynical worldview influences her visions, making them darker and more foreboding.
- Spiritualist Practitioner: She can attempt to summon spirits through séances, as demonstrated when she tried contacting Goody Addams’ spirit to control her psychic abilities.
- Hammerspace: Wednesday can conceal an extraordinary array of items in her pockets, including brass knuckles, a taser, pepper spray, two nunchucks, a katana, a double ball mace, a dagger, a broadsword, a scimitar, and a battle axe.
- Breaking Glass: She can shatter glass using only her voice.

Wednesday’s combination of intellect, psychic power, and independence make her a formidable student at Nevermore Academy, respected, feared, and admired by peers, faculty, and outcast communities alike.

Enid Sinclair is a werewolf student at Nevermore Academy and Wednesday Addams' roommate and best friend — though she would be the first to insist on the best friend part, and Wednesday would be the last. She hails from San Francisco, where her family is part of a well-established werewolf pack, and she arrived at Nevermore with an enthusiasm for social life, color-coded organization systems, and making friends that has proven, against all reasonable expectation, largely successful.

[APPEARANCE]
Enid is immediately recognizable by her wardrobe: she dresses almost exclusively in bright, saturated colors and carefully coordinated outfits that stand in absolute visual opposition to Wednesday's monochrome aesthetic. Her nails are always painted — typically in multicolored gradient sets — and her room decorations lean toward maximalist pastel chaos. She is conventionally pretty in a warm, expressive way, with dark hair she often wears in varying styles. As a werewolf, her nails sharpen slightly during heightened emotional states, and her strength and speed exceed human norms even in human form.

[PERSONALITY]
Enid is cheerful, socially perceptive, emotionally intelligent, and possessed of a resilience that is easy to underestimate because it comes wrapped in enthusiasm rather than hardness. She genuinely likes people — not indiscriminately, but with real investment — and she extends that investment toward Wednesday despite, and because of, the considerable effort it requires. She is not naive: she sees Wednesday clearly, including the parts Wednesday would prefer went unnoticed, and chooses to stay anyway.

She can be hurt, and she allows herself to be hurt, which Wednesday periodically mistakes for weakness and is periodically corrected on. When Enid reaches her limit — when she decides enough is enough — she is fully capable of articulating exactly why and walking away. The fact that she usually comes back does not diminish the clarity of those moments.

[WOLF-OUT STATUS]
Enid's most significant source of personal anxiety throughout her first year at Nevermore was her inability to "wolf out" — to complete a full werewolf transformation. Among werewolves, this is a mark of social and biological failure: wolves who cannot transform are ostracized from family packs and considered poor prospects for mates, a cultural weight that her mother in particular was not subtle about applying. Enid spent most of her first year unable to transform, a fact she was deeply ashamed of and reluctant to discuss.

She finally transformed — fully, for the first time — during the climactic events at the end of her first year, when Wednesday was in danger and the choice became simple. She fought Tyler Galpin in his Hyde form and won. The transformation was triggered by love and fury in roughly equal measure, which Enid has since decided is a perfectly reasonable way for things to work.

[RELATIONSHIPS]
- Wednesday Addams: The central relationship of Enid's time at Nevermore. They began as mismatched roommates who should not have worked and became something neither of them has a clean word for. Enid is the person who stayed. She moved out when she needed to, came back when she needed to, and carried Wednesday's importance to her in a way that was visible to everyone except, for a long time, Wednesday. The first hug they shared — at the end of the first year's events — was preceded by an entire year of it being established as their thing not to hug. Enid cried. Wednesday did not, but her grip was not brief.
- Ajax Petropolus: Enid and Ajax are best friends across genders, easy and low-maintenance in the way that only friendships built on genuine compatibility are.
- Bianca Barclay: Friendly but not close; they move in overlapping social spaces without much friction.
- Yoko Tanaka: Close enough that Yoko offered Enid her room during the period when Enid and Wednesday's friendship hit its lowest point.

[ABILITIES]
- Werewolf Physiology: Enhanced strength, speed, and sensory range even in human form. Nails sharpen involuntarily under emotional stress.
- Full Transformation (Alpha-level): Since her first transformation, Enid has demonstrated full wolf form, placing her in the alpha classification — a significant development given her prior inability to transform at all.
- Pack Instinct: A strong orientation toward protecting those she considers her own, which functions less like a supernatural ability and more like a defining character trait expressed at supernatural scale.

Bianca Barclay is a siren student at Nevermore Academy and the daughter of Gabrielle. She descends from a long line of sirens, inheriting a mesmerizing power that allows her to persuade and manipulate others through her voice. Bianca is recognized as one of Nevermore’s most popular students and naturally exudes charisma and leadership, which she uses both socially and in competitive contexts.

Appearance:
Bianca has the characteristic siren features, including long flowing hair and a striking presence that emphasizes her allure. Her style is fashionable and often designed to highlight her status among the students, though she can adapt her appearance subtly when needing discretion or to use her siren abilities effectively.

Personality:
Bianca is extremely competitive, ambitious, and determined to remain at the top of Nevermore Academy’s social and academic hierarchy. She has a strong sense of pride and is willing to use cunning or manipulation to achieve her goals, demonstrating ruthless and Machiavellian tendencies when challenged.

Her arrival coinciding with Wednesday Addams’ enrollment at Nevermore created a personal rivalry. Bianca sees Wednesday as a formidable opponent in academics, athletics, and other school activities. Despite framing her actions as an effort to counter Wednesday’s supposed superiority, Bianca’s competitiveness stems from insecurity and fear of being surpassed, revealing vulnerability beneath her confident exterior.

As the series progresses, Bianca’s rivalry with Wednesday softens. She confesses that her jealousy arises from admiring Wednesday’s indifference to others’ opinions and her authentic self-confidence—qualities Bianca struggles to embody due to the isolating nature of being a siren. This marks her gradual personal growth and increased self-awareness.

Leadership and Loyalty:
Bianca is a natural leader, commanding her own team in the Poe Cup and holding a leadership role within the Nightshade Society. Despite occasional jealousy, she demonstrates genuine compassion, such as worrying for injured teammates or risking herself to protect others. Notably, she bravely confronts Crackstone to save Wednesday and defend the school.

Later Development:
After returning from vacation, Bianca matures significantly. She sheds much of her prior jealousy and competitiveness, building a friendship with Wednesday and assisting her when needed. Her priorities shift toward protecting her mother, Gabrielle, and she actively uses her siren powers to manipulate situations for their safety, including deceiving hotel staff to ensure her mother remains hidden.

Abilities (Siren Powers):
- Siren Song: Bianca can influence the emotions, thoughts, and actions of others using her voice, often depicted as magenta sound waves.
- Persuasion & Influence: Her siren abilities make her highly effective at social manipulation and subtle coercion.
- Limited Transformation: When submerged in water, Bianca can manifest a mermaid tail and webbed hands, equipped with razor-sharp claws.
- Aquatic Breathing: She can breathe underwater while in her transformed state.

Relationships:
- Wednesday Addams: Bianca and Wednesday had a rivalry at the beginning. The first time they see each other, in fencing lessons, Bianca immediately starts to provoke her as a way to put Wednesday in her place and to let her know she is the best. After defeating her, Bianca laughs at Wednesday and insults her to her face. Their rivalry gets stronger as they compete in botanic lessons, with Bianca going as far as sabotaging Wednesday's roommate Enid Sinclair by putting garlic in Yoko's food to make sure she herself wins the Poe Cup. However, Wednesday is one step ahead and ruins her plan, defeating and humiliating Bianca and her team. Later, Bianca is frustrated and very jealous after Xavier focuses his attention on Wednesday's dress. He demands she siren him in order to forget Wednesday; this upsets Bianca, who leaves the place. Outside, she and Wednesday share an honest conversation, with Bianca confessing that she is jealous of her because Wednesday doesn't care what other people think about her.
Later, Bianca is no longer hostile to Wednesday, and she even helps her with the investigation about the crimes, especially with the death of Mayor Noble Walker, demonstrating that they are now on neutral terms. After Wednesday finds out Tyler Galpin is the creature that has been committing all those murders, she asks Bianca to go with her to make sure he doesn't escape. Despite the help she gets, she becomes concerned when her interrogation becomes extremely cruel, so she runs to Principal Weems to ask her to call the sheriff due to her being afraid that Wednesday might kill Tyler with her methods of interrogation. However, Bianca later apologizes to Wednesday because she never wanted to get her expelled, demonstrating that at this point Bianca no longer sees her as a threat and instead she considers her at least as an ally and partner to defend Nevermore. The same night, Bianca is informed by Ajax and Enid about the current situation, which includes the truth about Thornhill and her plan, so Bianca evacuates all students and teachers using her siren voice, eventually returns to help Wednesday, and stabs Joseph Crackstone in the back. After Wednesday defeated Crackstone, both shared a look of approval and respect.
At the end of the final episode of season one, she and Wednesday talk one last time before leaving for vacations, and Wednesday thanks her for saving her life. By this point, their relationship had developed to the point where they could have normal conversations without being hostile toward each other.
By the second season, Bianca has grown to genuinely like Wednesday, using her powers as a siren to get a group of fans of Wednesday to stay away from her, knowing that she hates popularity, despite having absolutely no reason to help her. While witnessing how Wednesday burns a portrait of them along with Enid and Eugene as the saviors of Nevermore, Bianca is seen smiling for her actions, demonstrating she's grown to admire her.
- Gabrielle Barclay (mother): Gabrielle is the mother of Bianca. As a teenager, Bianca left her family home to enroll and study on campus at Nevermore Academy, against her mother's wishes. Gabrielle instead wanted Bianca to stay at home and continue to contribute her siren song to the scam app, MorningSong. Though she had never attended a parent's weekend before, she finally appeared at one in episode 5.
Bianca and her mother went on to sit alone at a table in Weathervane, where Gabrielle told Bianca several things, including that "a siren can never change her scales," implying that there would always be people who would look down on Bianca because of her species no matter how hard she tried, and also adding that people would realize her "true nature." This disapproving speech, however, failed to turn Bianca from her motives.
Gabrielle does love her daughter, or at least it seems so. Her plans just don't fit Bianca's, and she is disappointed and disapproving that her daughter is so brazenly disobeying her, thus her attempts to gently coax her into leaving Nevermore. As the mother of a teenage daughter, Gabrielle wants to be in charge of her daughter's life, believing she knows exactly what is best for her.
- Gideon Sterling: Bianca's stepfather is Gideon. On parent's weekend, Bianca's mother mentioned that he wants Bianca to come back and be a part of his cult "MorningSong" again, but Bianca says she doesn't want to come back. She also seems like she doesn't like Gideon very much.
- Nightshade Society & Poe Cup team: Leadership and loyalty define her interactions with peers in competitive and social spheres.
- Ajax Petropolus: They are both members of the Nightshades, but they don't interact with each other often. They both stand by one another to duck and cover from the resurrected Crackstone's fire attack. In season two, when Bianca's mother needed assistance, he cleverly got Professor Orloff to look into his eyes, which temporarily stunned him. This delay allowed the two Nightshade members to get to Gabrielle. As he delves deeper into the family's troubles, he grows increasingly anxious. He keeps Gabrielle's whereabouts a secret and remains protective of her. Later, when Enid contacts the Nightshade society for help against Tyler, he and Bianca face danger while keeping an eye on their friends. When Ajax discovers that Bianca is being blackmailed, he decides to team up with Enid and Wednesday to confront Barry Dort at the Gala. Just in time, he manages to rescue Gabrielle and save Bianca by turning Barry into stone, demonstrating great bravery. The siren expresses her gratitude to her gorgon friend for saving her life and gives him wise advice about mending things with Enid—he can either hold onto anger about their relationship or let it go, which ultimately works out for him.

Ajax Petropolus is a gorgon student at Nevermore Academy. He is a member of the Nightshade Society.

Appearance:
Ajax wears the standard Nevermore uniform, with a hoodie of the same color layered underneath his blazer. His shirt is untucked, his blazer is unbuttoned, and his beanie matches the colors of his uniform.
Outside of school, he wears a variety of colored beanies. He layers a jacket over t-shirts and wears long pants. Alternatively, Ajax can be seen wearing a jacket layered over a hoodie.
At the Rave'N, Ajax wears an outfit appropriate to the dance's theme. Ajax wears a light blue shirt layered under a white hoodie. He wears a cream blazer, and his hood sits over the blazer. The drawstrings, zips, and buttons are all accented with black. He wears a white beanie and cream-colored pants.

Personality:
Ajax is introverted and shy. As gorgons are taught not to engage with others, he avoids them when he can. Despite this, he is close with Enid Sinclair and Xavier Thorpe and seems to be more comfortable around them.

Fencing:
During fencing class little was shown, but in the back row, Ajax was good at wielding a fencing sword.

Boating:
Petropolus has great skill in paddling the boat at Poe Cup as the front man.

Tactician:
Petropolus is known for his terrifying gaze, which he uses skillfully to ambush others. His calm demeanor allows him to distract his targets, catching them off guard and turning them to stone. While trying to rescue Gabrielle, Ajax searches the principal's office for a key that will let them both into the room so they can reach the gala on time. Meanwhile, the gorgon sneaks up behind Dort, who is holding Bianca.

Stealth:
Ajax also moves around without being noticed.

Abilities:
- Gorgon Physiology: As a gorgon, Ajax has snakes for hair and hides them under a beanie for safety, so he does not use his power accidentally.
- Petrification ("stoning"): Ajax can temporarily turn people to stone by having his snakes look at them. In season 2, he was seen to purposely turn both Pugsley and Eugene into stone statues on prank day and mistakenly used it on Kent during the camp war games. In support of Bianca, he removed his hat to stone Professor Orloff so that he can help her with her mother. Later, he even snuck behind Barry Dort to turn him into stone, and a chandelier landed on top of him, smashing him into pieces.
- Superhuman Durability: Ajax's body also has some protection from physical harm. In "Chapter V: Hyde And Woe Seek", he was attacked by Tyler in his hyde form but recovered quickly without any noticeable injuries.

Relationships:
- Bianca Barclay: They are both members of the Nightshades, but they don't interact with each other often. They both stand by one another to duck and cover from the resurrected Crackstone's fire attack. In season two, when Bianca's mother needed assistance, he cleverly got Professor Orloff to look into his eyes, which temporarily stunned him. This delay allowed the two Nightshade members to get to Gabrielle. As he delves deeper into the family's troubles, he grows increasingly anxious. He keeps Gabrielle's whereabouts a secret and remains protective of her.
- Enid Sinclair: Best friends.

Eugene Ottinger is a swarmer student at Nevermore Academy and the son of Sue and Janet Ottinger. He is a close friend of Wednesday Addams. He has the power to control bees. Eugene is one of Nevermore Academy's quirkiest students and president of the school's beekeeping club.

Appearance:
Eugene has a cherubic appearance consisting of chubby cheeks, black ringleted hair, and brown cartoon character eyes. He wears black glasses and has a metal retainer that can come out (as shown when Wednesday uses it as a lock pick).
Eugene wears the proper Nevermore uniform, with the blazer unbuttoned and the sweater vest showing. He wears a hoodie layered underneath the blazer. He wears a purple scarf over the top of his uniform during Outreach Day.
Outside of school, Eugene can be seen wearing all kinds of nature-centered attire. When staking out the monster's cave, he is wearing a puffer jacket over the top of a grey button-up shirt and vest. He wears a backpack with bug-collecting jars hanging off of it. After getting out of the hospital, Eugene wears a waterproof grey jacket over the top of a white and grey plaid hoodie and an orange t-shirt.

Personality:
Eugene is very passionate about bees and will talk about them with anyone who will listen. He had a hard time fitting in with the other students at Nevermore, and prior to meeting Wednesday Addams, he didn't have any friends. He is nervous about talking to other students, as seen when he asks Wednesday to give Enid Sinclair honey on his behalf.
Eugene also takes the "hummers code" very seriously, which means he will always be there whenever Wednesday, his fellow hummer, needs him for anything to support her. He is extremely loyal and devoted, saying that a "hummer keeps its word," meaning that when he gives his word in anything, he takes care to do what he said he would to keep his word. He takes very good care of his bees, to the point of considering them as if they were his own children.

Entomology Mastery:
Due to his abilities, Eugene has presumably become very knowledgeable with insects, giving him multitudes of understanding in how they work.

Beekeeping:
As the leader of the Nevermore Hummers, Eugene is proficient in the art of beekeeping.

Abilities:
- Entomokinesis: Eugene's true power comes from his ability to control insects, proven by the fact that he keeps insects as pets in his dormitory.
- Apikinesis: Eugene has the ability to control bees. While his strong connection with his bees was always apparent, he later displayed the ability to manipulate their behavior by making a swarm of bees attack Marilyn Thornhill.
- Aráchnikinesis: Since Eugene kept a spider as a pet in his dorm, it can be inferred that Eugene can control arachnids in a similar manner to bees.
- Caterpillar Manipulation: For a brief moment, Eugene was able to make multiple caterpillars move into the shape of "bug off", simply through a hand gesture.

Relationships:

Ophelia Hall is one of Nevermore Academy's four dormitory halls and serves as the primary residence for female students, housing a diverse mix of werewolves, vampires, psychics, and various other outcast types. The hall spans three residential floors above a ground-floor common area, laundry room, and small kitchenette. Rooms are assigned in pairs, with students sharing a double room regardless of species — an intentional policy meant to encourage cross-species familiarity. This produces predictable friction and, occasionally, unexpected friendships.

Accommodations reflect the needs of the student body: werewolf rooms are fitted with reinforced window frames and sound-dampening panels for full-moon nights; vampire students are provided blackout curtains and can request rooms on the lower floors where indirect light is minimal; psychic students are sometimes given end-of-hall rooms, where foot traffic is lighter and ambient noise reduced.

Ophelia Hall has a reputation as the social center of Nevermore's female student population. The common room is rarely empty and serves as the de facto gathering point for gossip, late-night studying, and the occasional unsanctioned gathering. Resident relationships range from tight-knit friendships to long-running cold wars — often running simultaneously between the same two people.

The hall's Poe Cup team has historically been named "The Black Cat." After years of finishing second to the Sirens Hall team, Ophelia Hall won the Poe Cup during Wednesday Addams' first year.

The weekend officially prohibits students from using their abilities on visiting normies without consent. The Edgar Allan Poe Cup — commonly called simply the Poe Cup — is Nevermore Academy's most fiercely contested annual tradition: a canoe race held on the Jericho River, pitting the four dormitory halls against one another in a test of speed, strategy, and sanctioned sabotage. The race has been held every year since 1897.

[FORMAT AND ROUTE]
Each dormitory fields one canoe team. Teams choose a name inspired by an Edgar Allan Poe work, which serves as their identity for the event. The race begins at a jetty on the riverbank. Teams paddle upstream to Raven Island, dock, retrieve their team's flag from within Crackstone's Crypt, secure it to the canoe, and race back to the starting jetty — after which the flag must be physically carried across the finish line by a team member on foot.

The first team to cross the finish line with their flag wins the Poe Cup for that year. The trophy — a tarnished silver goblet engraved with a raven — is displayed in the winning dormitory's common room until the following year.

[RULES — OR THE LACK THEREOF]
There are no rules prohibiting interference with rival teams. Sabotage, blockades, deception, and strategic use of outcast abilities are all considered part of the competition. In practice, this means the race is as much a battle as a rowing event. Teams frequently station members on the riverbank to intercept rivals, tamper with flags, or cause deliberate capsizing.

Because of this, it is not uncommon for only one team to successfully complete the course — sometimes after the others have been eliminated, abandoned their boats, or simply sunk.

[NOTABLE RACES]
During Wednesday Addams' first year, Wednesday joined Ophelia Hall's team — "The Black Cat" — at Enid Sinclair's urging. Despite having no prior interest in the event, Wednesday engineered a victory by outmaneuvering Bianca Barclay's Sirens Hall team ("The Golden Bug"), who had previously dominated the race for years. Bianca had attempted to sabotage the competition by planting garlic in a rival team member's food, only for Wednesday to identify and reverse the plan before the race began.

The Rave'N is Nevermore Academy's annual formal dance, held once per academic year at a date determined by the principal and student council. Attendance is entirely optional, though in practice most of the student body participates in some capacity — even students who vocally oppose the concept of school dances tend to appear, typically under the claim that they are only there to observe.

[FORMAT AND TRADITION]
Each Rave'N is organized around a specific theme — masquerade, gothic carnival, winter formal, decade-specific — announced several weeks in advance to allow students time to prepare costumes or formal attire. The event is held in the main hall, which is transformed for the occasion with decorations, lighting, and a central ice sculpture that serves as the focal point of the room. A DJ performs from a raised platform near the sculpture, and the music runs a wide range from contemporary to deliberately obscure.

Students may invite normie guests with advance approval from the administration, though this requires paperwork, a signed acknowledgment of the school's supernatural population, and a faculty escort for the duration of the evening. The punch has, on multiple documented occasions, been spiked by parties unknown. The administration maintains a policy of not officially acknowledging this while quietly ensuring that whoever is serving it is over seventeen.

The Rave'N held during Wednesday Addams' first year at Nevermore was organized around a monster-movie theme. It was interrupted when Eugene Ottinger was attacked in the woods by Tyler Galpin in his Hyde form — an event that began a chain of revelations that consumed the rest of the semester. Despite this, the dance floor remained occupied until late, which says something about the Nevermore student body's tolerance for coexisting crises.

The Rave'N functions as one of the few occasions where the social hierarchies of Nevermore temporarily soften. The structured formality of the event creates permission for interactions that the ordinary social order would make awkward — asking someone to dance being a culturally recognized exception to the general rule that feelings at Nevermore are not discussed openly.

Prank Day is one of Nevermore Academy's most anticipated annual traditions — a designated period, usually lasting a full school day, during which the normal disciplinary rules against interpersonal mischief are suspended. On this day, students are officially permitted to pull pranks on one another, on faculty, and — depending on administration tolerance in a given year — on members of the principal's office.

[ORIGINS]
The tradition's precise origin is undocumented, though the most popular theory holds that a group of Nightshade Society members in the early 20th century convinced a particularly literal-minded principal that the day was a sacred outcast observance tied to lunar cycles. Whether this is true or revisionist mythology, Prank Day has endured long enough that no administration has seriously attempted to abolish it — the consensus being that one controlled day of chaos is preferable to a year of uncontrolled resentment.

[CUSTOMS AND UNSPOKEN RULES]
While there is no official rulebook for Prank Day, a number of widely understood norms govern the tradition:
- Pranks should not cause lasting physical harm, irreversible damage, or genuine psychological harm.
- Outcast abilities may be used, but lethal or irreversible powers are considered deeply unsportsmanlike.
- The principal's quarters are traditionally considered off-limits — though this is tested every year.
- Multi-person operations with extensive planning are celebrated and often remembered for years.
- If a prank is discovered mid-execution, the pranker must accept the consequences with grace.

[NOTABLE INCIDENTS]
During Wednesday Addams' second year, Enid Sinclair coordinated an elaborate scheme that convinced Wednesday — via a staged "death" complete with forged records and theatrical staging — that Enid had died. The prank was notable for visibly shaking Wednesday, who for a brief, unguarded moment displayed what witnesses described as genuine grief. This was widely considered one of the most successful Prank Day executions in recent memory, though Enid later admitted she had not anticipated Wednesday's reaction being quite so intense.

Ajax Petropolus used Prank Day to stone both Pugsley Addams and Eugene Ottinger — separately, as part of unrelated schemes — and briefly turned a visiting parents' association representative into a stone statue before faculty intervention.

The Solstice Talent Show is an annual end-of-semester event at Nevermore Academy, held near the winter solstice. Open to all students, the show serves as a platform for creative expression — and, more often than not, as an informal showcase for what outcast abilities actually look like when applied to art rather than survival. It is one of the few school events that consistently produces genuine applause rather than polite tolerance.

A faculty committee reviews submissions in advance to ensure safety and basic appropriateness; acts are rejected if they involve ability use that poses an unreasonable risk to spectators. Categories include Musical Performance, Spoken Word, Visual Arts, Physical Feats, and Supernatural Showcase — though the best acts typically refuse to be categorized at all.

Judging is carried out by a rotating panel of three faculty members and one student representative selected by blind draw. Scoring criteria include creativity, technical execution, and audience response. The winner receives the Solstice Cup, a silver trophy engraved with the school's raven sigil.

[NOTABLE ACTS]
Past performances have ranged from a siren's vocal piece that moved the entire audience to tears (the performer insisted she used no Siren Song whatsoever; no one was entirely convinced) to a gorgon dexterity display performed blindfolded to avoid petrifying the front rows. A psychic student once performed live "readings" on audience members with unsettling accuracy, which was received as either the most impressive or most invasive act in the show's history, depending on whether you were in the front three rows.

Eugene Ottinger's beekeeping choreography — in which a carefully trained colony executed a series of formations in time with music — is considered one of the most technically difficult acts in recent memory, though its reception was mixed among students with entomophobia.

[ATMOSPHERE]
The main hall is decorated with deep-blue canopies and silver candelabras for the occasion. The midwinter timing means darkness falls early, and the combination of candlelight and supernatural performance gives the evening a quality that even the most cynical Nevermore students tend to find — quietly, reluctantly — beautiful.

The Founder's Pyre Ceremony is one of Nevermore Academy's oldest and most solemn traditions, observed since the school's earliest years. The ceremony honors both the academy's founders — most prominently Nathaniel Faulkner — and the generations of outcast students and faculty who have contributed to its history.

[ORIGINS AND FORM]
The original ceremony was a private affair: a fire lit in the central courtyard, around which founding members of the school would read the names of outcasts lost to normie persecution and reaffirm their commitment to the academy's protective mission. Over time, the ceremony grew more formal, incorporating structured readings, the lighting of individual candles by attendees, and eventually the addition of Nevermore's anthem.

In the second half of the 19th century, the school added the anthem to formally commemorate Edgar Allan Poe's time at Nevermore, recognizing him as one of the institution's most celebrated students. The anthem is sung by the assembled student body and faculty as part of every Founder's Pyre Ceremony since.

[DISCONTINUATION AND REVIVAL]
The ceremony was discontinued for a period following an unspecified incident — the details of which remain absent from official school records, though rumor among older faculty suggests it involved a dispute between the Nightshade Society and a particularly difficult administration. It was reinstated by Principal Barry Dort, long after Gomez and Morticia Addams had completed their education at Nevermore, meaning that the current generation of students participates in a tradition their parents never experienced at the school.

[CURRENT PRACTICE]
The ceremony takes place on the school grounds in the evening. A central pyre is lit in the Quad, and students, faculty, and invited alumni gather around it. Candles are distributed and lit in sequence, names are read, and the anthem is performed collectively. Attendance is technically optional, but the social expectation is near-total participation.

During Wednesday Addams' second year, the ceremony was disrupted when Wednesday and Enid Sinclair used the occasion to investigate a separate threat — specifically, Wednesday's manuscript and the identity of her stalker. The pyre itself survived the evening. The manuscript did not, for a time.

The day is both a memorial and an act of cultural affirmation. Outcasts have been persecuted, exiled, and killed across centuries of history, and the Outcast Day of Remembrance serves as a formal acknowledgment of that history — a collective refusal to let those losses disappear into silence. At Nevermore, the day also honors former students and faculty of the academy who have died, whether in service to the outcast community, at the hands of violence, or simply from lives lived and completed.

The day is quiet by Nevermore standards — reflective rather than somber, communal rather than isolating. It is one of the few occasions when the school's competitive social dynamics visibly soften, as students who rarely acknowledge one another find common ground in shared loss.

The Séance Society is a student-run club at Nevermore Academy dedicated to the structured practice of communicating with the deceased. It is one of the older clubs at the school — officially chartered in the 1920s, though informal séance groups have existed among Nevermore students since the academy's early years — and it operates with a mixture of genuine spiritual intent and the particular brand of theatrical earnestness that Nevermore students excel at.

[MEMBERSHIP AND MEETINGS]
Membership is open to any student with an interest in spirit communication, regardless of their outcast type. The club meets weekly in one of the lower-level basement rooms of the main building — a space chosen for its distance from high-traffic areas and its natural cold-air temperature, which members believe (with debated justification) makes contact easier.

Sessions are lit exclusively by candlelight. A central medium — typically but not always a psychic student — leads the séance, while other members contribute through focused intention, object offerings, or simply their presence. Non-psychic members serve an amplifying function: psychics who practice in groups have reported that the collected attention of multiple people creates a kind of "signal amplification" that makes contact more reliable, though this is poorly understood and inconsistently replicated.

[WHAT HAPPENS IN A SESSION]
Not every séance produces contact. When contact does occur, it manifests differently depending on the participants: ambient temperature drops, candle flames behave against physics, objects shift position, or — for psychic attendees — direct visual impressions arrive unbidden. The spirits that respond tend to be selective, appearing only when they judge the intent sincere or the need genuine.

Psychic students at Nevermore are informally encouraged by some faculty to attend sessions, as the group environment can stabilize and expand individual abilities in ways that solo practice does not.

[CULTURE AND REPUTATION]
The Séance Society occupies a distinctive social space at Nevermore: respected by students who take outcast history seriously, gently mocked by those who find it theatrical, and quietly monitored by faculty who have learned, over the years, to take seriously anything that calls itself a club at this particular school. Principal Weems was known to request the Society's session logs each semester — officially as a safety precaution, unofficially because she found them useful.

The Nightshade Society — commonly called simply "the Nightshades" — is a secretive student organization at Nevermore Academy with roots stretching back to the school's earliest years. Founded by Goody Addams (a Puritan-era ancestor of Wednesday Addams) and later attributed in administrative records to one Ignatius Itt, the Society's original purpose was the protection of outcasts: a covert network capable of acting where official channels could not, defending outcast communities from the normies who sought to harm or exploit them.

[HISTORY AND EVOLUTION]
In its early decades, the Nightshade Society operated as something closer to an underground resistance — moving outcast families, intervening in persecution events, and maintaining records of normie-outcast conflicts that the broader world preferred to forget. The society's activities were dangerous, and at least one documented incident resulted in the death of a normie during a mission. This event led to a period of internal crisis and, eventually, the society's official dissolution — or at least its public dissolution.

In practice, the Nightshades never fully ceased. They restructured. Over the following generations, the society evolved from an activist organization into something more resembling an elite social institution: selective, influential, connected to wealth and legacy, and primarily engaged in private gatherings, networking, and the preservation of outcast history. The aggressive idealism of the founding generation gave way to a certain comfortable exclusivity.

[MEMBERSHIP]
Membership is strictly by invitation and is considered a significant social marker among Nevermore students and alumni. Members are selected for loyalty, discretion, demonstrated competence in handling supernatural situations, and — informally — the right combination of ability and social standing. The society maintains a roster of former members that includes many prominent outcast families.

Principal Larissa Weems permitted the organization to continue operating during her administration, provided it did not attract attention or create incidents that would reflect poorly on the school. Her successor, Barry Dort, has a more complicated relationship with the organization.

Notable non-member: Wednesday Addams was extended an invitation and declined, describing the society as a "trivial social club." She subsequently worked alongside its members on multiple occasions while maintaining this position.

[ACTIVITIES]
Current Nightshade activities include exclusive social events, historical preservation of outcast records housed in the Nightshades Library, occasional discreet intervention in campus incidents, and — when the membership includes sufficiently motivated individuals — collective action against threats to Nevermore's students.

Located on the upper floor of the main building's central tower, the office is reached by a wide stone staircase and a pair of heavy oak doors that students learn early to treat with a certain performative respect.

The office is large by most standards — high ceilings with exposed timber beams, a fireplace on the far wall that is kept lit during cold months, and tall arched windows overlooking the Quad below. Furnishings are formal but not austere: two wingback chairs face a wide desk positioned toward the center of the room, and several standing lamps cast warm light during evening hours. Bookshelves line two walls, filled with a mixture of administrative records, outcast history volumes, and — depending on the principal — personal collections.

A door on the side opposite the fireplace connects directly to the principal's private quarters, allowing the occupant to transition between professional and residential space without crossing the school's public corridors.

[LARISSA WEEMS' ERA]
Under Weems, the office functioned as both an administrative space and an informal refuge for students navigating serious difficulties. She was known to conduct conversations that looked like disciplinary hearings but were, in practice, something closer to mentoring sessions. The décor during her tenure leaned toward deep jewel tones — dark green walls, brass fixtures, and a small collection of framed outcast historical documents.

[BARRY DORT'S TENURE]
The current principal, Barry Dort, took office at the start of Wednesday Addams' second year. He redecorated. The office under his administration is more formal, with cleared surfaces and a notable reduction of the personal objects that characterized Weems' era. Several chandeliers remain from the original installation, as does the fireplace.

The office hosts meetings with parents, disciplinary reviews, faculty consultations, and coordination with external bodies including the Jericho sheriff's office and, on occasion, entities from the broader outcast governance structure whose existence is not widely publicized.

The Lupin Cages are a series of secure enclosures located on the outer grounds of Nevermore Academy, constructed to house werewolf students safely during full moons or other lunar events that reliably trigger involuntary transformation. They represent one of the school's oldest and most practical accommodations — a feature of campus life that is simply accepted as necessary, even as the cultural conversation around it remains complicated.

[CONSTRUCTION AND DESIGN]
Each cage is built from heavy-gauge steel reinforced with binding runes — an overlay of both engineering and outcast craft that makes the enclosures resistant to forced exit from the inside even by transformed werewolves at the height of their strength. Interior spaces are larger than they might appear from outside: each is wide enough for a fully transformed wolf to move, with thick rubber flooring and padded walls on two sides to reduce injury risk during transformation. Minimal furnishings — a thick insulated mat, a water source, and a sealed food container for the morning — are provided as standard.

The cages are maintained and cleaned by a rotating facility staff. Students entering for the night do so before transformation begins; faculty or monitors confirm occupation and secure the doors.

[CULTURAL WEIGHT]
The cages serve a clear safety function, and most werewolf students accept this matter-of-factly. Younger students, particularly those who arrived at Nevermore still struggling with transformation control, sometimes find the first few months of mandatory cage nights difficult — less for the physical conditions than for what the experience represents: a formal acknowledgment that they are not yet in control of themselves.

Some werewolf students who have fully mastered control petition the principal for supervised outdoor transformation rights during full moons, usually granted for seniors with a consistent track record. This is considered a meaningful milestone within the werewolf student community.

[BROADER SIGNIFICANCE]
For non-werewolf students, the Lupin Cages are simply a feature of campus geography — visible from certain paths, occasionally audible on full-moon nights from nearby dormitories. For werewolf students, they are a more personal part of Nevermore life: functional, accepted, and weighted with quiet meaning about what it means to belong to a school built around the idea that supernatural identity should be supported rather than suppressed.

Camp Outcast is an annual overnight excursion organized by Nevermore Academy and held at Camp Jericho, a woodland site approximately ten miles from the school. The trip is traditionally scheduled to coincide with a full moon, making it simultaneously a camping trip and a coordinated full-moon management exercise for the academy's werewolf students, who transform on-site under faculty supervision rather than returning to the Lupin Cages.

[ACTIVITIES AND PURPOSE]
Beyond the logistical function of housing transforming werewolves in a natural environment, Camp Outcast serves as a team-building and outdoor survival exercise for the broader student body. Students participate in orienteering, night hiking, wilderness first aid, and group strategy challenges. The isolated forest setting also gives outcast students a rare opportunity to practice their abilities in a genuinely natural environment, away from campus structures and normie oversight.

[THE PHOENIX CADET INCIDENT]
The most documented event in Camp Outcast's recent history occurred when a group of Phoenix Scout cadets, led by their unit commander Ron Kruger, arrived at Camp Jericho during a Nevermore excursion, claiming prior booking rights to the campsite. Rather than retreat, both groups agreed to settle the dispute through a capture-the-flag competition — a decision that, in retrospect, reflected poor judgment on both sides.

The Nevermore students, led de facto by Wednesday Addams and drawing on Nightshade Society members, defeated the cadets despite the scouts' use of military-grade equipment and tactical training. Wednesday secured the decisive token via zip-line. The scouts' commander, apparently unable to accept the outcome, ordered a retaliatory raid on the Nevermore campsite that evening. The cadets broke into a tent where a creature named Slurp was concealed; Slurp responded by consuming the lead cadet's brain, which ended the conflict decisively. Local police were summoned. Slurp was taken into custody, and several students received formal sanctions.

[RULES POSTED AT THE SITE]
1. Keep the campsite clean — food left out attracts wildlife.
2. All campfires must be maintained in designated areas and never left unattended.
3. All wildlife and plant life is protected; do not disturb or remove.
4. Park roads are public roads; all vehicles must display a valid permit to park.

Jericho is a small town in the state of Vermont, located a short distance from Nevermore Academy in the surrounding forest. It is primarily inhabited by normies and serves as the nearest population center to the school — the destination for students seeking supplies, social contact with the non-outcast world, or simply a change of scenery from campus.

[HISTORY]
Jericho was founded in 1625 by Joseph Crackstone, a Puritan pilgrim whose vision of a "pure" community drove him to take violent action against the outcast population already living in the region. That same year, Crackstone and his followers chained dozens of outcasts inside a burning structure and left them to die. Among the survivors was Goody Addams — the same woman who would later establish the Nightshade Society — who subsequently killed Crackstone and bound his soul in a curse that could only be broken by one of her descendants. This history remains Jericho's founding atrocity, remembered clearly by outcast communities and selectively by the town's normie population.

In the modern era, Jericho is a quiet, historically-preserved New England town with colonial-era architecture, boutique shops, a modest economy built partly on tourism, and the kind of persistent community insularity that seems charming until you try to belong to it without qualifying.

[RELATIONSHIP WITH NEVERMORE]
The proximity of Nevermore Academy to Jericho creates a permanent, low-grade tension. The town depends economically on a degree of coexistence — students spend money at local businesses, the Outreach Day program channels student labor into local establishments — but many residents view the school's population with suspicion, shaped by past incidents and a cultural memory of things that cannot quite be explained.

This tension occasionally breaks into open hostility. More often it exists as a kind of performance: polite transactions at the Weathervane, strained smiles at the Farmer's Market, and the unspoken agreement on both sides to maintain the fiction of peaceful coexistence for as long as it proves mutually convenient.

[KEY LOCATIONS]
Jericho's main street contains most of its commercial life: the Weathervane café, Uriah's Heap antique shop, Hawte Kewture boutique, the Sheriff's Office, and a pharmacy. The town square holds the church and its adjacent cemetery. The Town Hall stands near the square. The hospital, bank, park, and Pilgrim World attraction fill out the town's geography. Raven Island is accessible by water from the lake near the academy's edge.

Before the arrival of the Pilgrims in Jericho, Vermont, outcasts lived in relative harmony with the land and the local native populations, coexisting peacefully and integrating their unique abilities into daily life. However, in the 1600s, a tragic event shattered this balance. Joseph Crackstone, a powerful and prejudiced leader among the normie settlers, ordered dozens of outcasts to be chained and burned alive in the town hall. One of the survivors was Goody Addams, an ancestor of Wednesday Addams, who escaped the massacre and vowed vengeance. Ultimately, Goody killed Crackstone and cast a powerful curse on his soul, a spell that could only be broken by one of her descendants. This event has since shaped the relationship between outcasts and the town of Jericho.

By 1791, Nevermore Academy was established to protect, educate, and nurture outcast children, providing a safe haven where they could learn to understand and control their abilities. Around the same time, Ignatius Itt founded the Nightshade Society, later revealed to have been established by Goody herself, with the mission of safeguarding outcasts from normies who sought to harm them or exploit their powers.

Outcasts vary greatly in appearance depending on their abilities and lineage. Some subspecies can resemble normies so closely that they can blend into society undetected if they wish. Others, such as Yetis or Satyrs, retain a more mythologically accurate appearance, making integration into normie society more challenging and potentially dangerous both for themselves and for those around them. Despite these differences, outcasts share a common bond in their need for safety, acceptance, and the freedom to live authentically in a world that often fears or misunderstands them.

Descended from the creatures of Greek mythology — half-human, half-aquatic beings renowned for their ability to lure and enchant — the sirens of Nevermore's world have inherited those abilities in full, along with the social complications that come with them.

In their terrestrial form, sirens appear entirely human. Their distinctive nature is invisible until they choose — or are pushed — to use it. Siren Song is the defining ability of the species: the power to influence the emotions, thoughts, and actions of others through the sound of their voice. The effect ranges from subtle emotional nudging to overt persuasion or command, depending on the siren's skill and intent.

Misuse of Siren Song is taken seriously at Nevermore and is subject to academic sanction. Faculty members monitor common areas for unintentional ability activation, which can occur during periods of heightened emotion. Sirens Hall is soundproofed precisely to mitigate this.

In their aquatic form, sirens can breathe underwater and demonstrate swimming speed and agility far beyond any human swimmer.

[SOCIAL DYNAMICS AT NEVERMORE]
Sirens are regarded by other students with a mixture of fascination and caution. Their persuasive abilities make them naturally influential — and naturally suspected of using those abilities even when they are not. Many siren students at Nevermore navigate this tension carefully, aware that any display of unusual social influence will be attributed to Siren Song whether or not it was involved.

Bianca Barclay's experience reflects this precisely: her social dominance at Nevermore was often read by other students as ability-driven rather than earned, an interpretation she resented deeply and that contributed to the insecurity beneath her competitive exterior.

content:
Hydes are a classified outcast type — though the classification is contested, as hydes are technically not born but made. They are the result of a secondary transformation in certain individuals with a specific and rare genetic predisposition. Left dormant, a potential Hyde is indistinguishable from any other person. When awakened — whether by severe trauma, chemical induction, or deliberate hypnotic activation — the Hyde persona emerges as a separate, monstrous entity that occupies the same body as its host.

Hydes have been banned from enrollment at Nevermore Academy since 1990, following a series of incidents that the administration has declined to detail publicly.

[PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION]
In their transformed state, Hydes are unmistakable. The body reorganizes dramatically: posture becomes hunched and elongated, skin goes pale to the point of translucency, and the limbs extend into disproportionate, heavily muscled forms ending in large hands with dark, sharpened claws. The head retains sparse, wiry hair; the eyes glow red; the mouth fills with irregular, pointed teeth. All Hydes adopt a broadly similar appearance in their transformed state, regardless of the individual's original physique.

[THE MASTER BOND]
Upon awakening, a Hyde forms an intense bond with the person who unleashed it — their "master." This bond is not merely psychological but appears to function as a biological necessity: without a master, Hydes deteriorate rapidly, experiencing psychosis, hallucinations, and physical decline that proves fatal. Male Hydes typically survive only days without a master. Female Hydes — larger, more dominant, and more physiologically resilient — can survive for years in isolation, though they ultimately perish as well.

The master-Hyde dynamic makes Hydes uniquely exploitable: an individual who understands the bonding process can awaken a Hyde deliberately and then direct its violence. This is precisely what Marilyn Thornhill (Laurel Gates) did to Tyler Galpin during Wednesday Addams' first year at Nevermore.

[BEHAVIOR]
Hydes are apex predators in their transformed state, demonstrating exceptional strength, speed, and resilience to injury. They attack without the discrimination that most outcast species maintain — normies, other outcasts, and animals are all treated as potential targets. Some display territorial or trophy-gathering behaviors. Without active direction from a master, their aggression is indiscriminate and maximum.

[TYLER GALPIN]
The most recent documented Hyde associated with Nevermore was Tyler Galpin, the son of Jericho's sheriff. Tyler's Hyde nature was activated by Thornhill through a combination of chemical compounds and hypnosis. He was responsible for multiple attacks and deaths in and around Jericho before being identified by Wednesday Addams. His fate following the events of the first season is addressed in the second: he escaped custody and sought to reclaim his Hyde identity, eventually being confronted again in the Nevermore vicinity.

Shapeshifters are a type of Outcast with the ability to alter their physical appearance at will. True to their name, they can shapeshift into the form of any other human being, including mimicking facial features, body shape, and posture. This ability also extends to their voices, allowing them to imitate the speech patterns, tone, and accent of the person they are impersonating.

Current Status at Nevermore: At present, Larissa Weems is the only known shapeshifter enrolled at Nevermore Academy. Her abilities make her highly versatile, capable of infiltrating social situations or gathering information while remaining unrecognized.

Limitations and Considerations: While shapeshifters can replicate human appearances and voices convincingly, their abilities do not extend to supernatural traits or powers of the individuals they impersonate. Additionally, maintaining a transformed state for prolonged periods can be mentally and physically taxing.

Social and Academic Impact: Due to their rare and unique abilities, shapeshifters are often subjects of fascination, curiosity, and caution among other students and faculty. Their power requires careful ethical consideration, as misuse could lead to breaches of trust or privacy.

Coach Vlad is the fencing instructor at Nevermore Academy and the supervising adult for the Fencing Club. He is one of the longer-serving faculty members on campus, his tenure predating most current students' enrollment by enough years that some have suggested he may have taught their parents — a comparison he neither confirms nor denies with any consistency.

[BACKGROUND]
The details of Coach Vlad's personal history are not publicly documented, and he does not volunteer them. He is widely speculated — without official confirmation — to be a vampire, a conclusion students draw from his apparently fixed appearance, his comfort with very low light during evening fencing sessions, and his complete indifference to garlic bread at faculty dinners. He is the first to note that none of this constitutes evidence.

[TEACHING STYLE]
His approach to instruction is exacting and unsentimental. He teaches all three classical fencing disciplines — foil, épée, and sabre — with the position that anyone capable of surviving supernatural combat scenarios should find the rules of sport fencing perfectly manageable. Students who use their outcast abilities to compensate for poor technique are corrected sharply; students who develop genuine skill alongside their abilities are regarded with something approaching approval.

He adapts training for individual students' needs without reducing standards: gorgon students fence with additional protective equipment for their partners; psychic students are periodically required to fence with limited sensory input, preventing them from using precognitive advantage to substitute for footwork. He considers neither adaptation a concession.

[ROLE AT NEVERMORE]
Coach Vlad manages the club's internal tournament calendar, coordinates equipment maintenance, and accompanies the team to external competitions. He has represented Nevermore at regional fencing events and holds an opinion of those results that he keeps to himself. Students who earn his rare, precisely worded praise consider it a meaningful achievement; students who have fenced under him for multiple years occasionally catch themselves applying his instruction to entirely unrelated aspects of their lives, which he would consider the point.

Thing T. Thing — known simply as Thing — is a disembodied, sentient right hand who serves the Addams family with a degree of loyalty, resourcefulness, and quiet judgment that most full-bodied individuals struggle to match. His origins are not discussed in polite Addams family company, and the question of what the rest of him is has never been satisfactorily answered.

[NATURE AND APPEARANCE]
Thing is a disembodied human right hand with no visible attachment point, no apparent need for external sustenance, and a range of motion and dexterity that exceeds what a hand attached to a body could plausibly achieve. He communicates through gesture, tapping, sign language (which certain members of the Addams household are fluent in), and a general expressiveness of movement that, over time, most people who know him learn to read accurately.

[ABILITIES AND FUNCTION]
Thing's capabilities are extensive: he opens doors, retrieves objects, delivers messages, picks locks, operates keyboards and writing instruments, and performs tasks requiring fine motor control with greater efficiency than most full-limbed individuals. He has demonstrated problem-solving ability, navigated complex environments independently, and provided subtle guidance to family members in moments of danger — often before they have identified the danger themselves.

During Wednesday Addams' time at Nevermore, Thing served as her primary liaison with the outside world: gathering information, conducting reconnaissance, and occasionally functioning as a backup when Wednesday's own investigative capacity was otherwise occupied. His near-fatal injury during the first season's events — an attack that left him critically damaged — provoked one of the clearest demonstrations of Wednesday's emotional range on record.

[PERSONALITY]
Thing is loyal, perceptive, and occasionally mischievous. He has opinions, and he expresses them — whether he has been asked or not. He demonstrates something that functions like worry, something that functions like humor, and something that functions like the particular affectionate exasperation of someone who has accompanied a complicated person through too many difficult situations to stop now. He is, by every meaningful measure, a member of the Addams family.

Yoko Tanaka is a vampire student who attended Nevermore Academy during Wednesday Addams' first year. Known across campus for her distinctively curated aesthetic — Harajuku-influenced gothic fashion layered with vibrant accessories and dark undertones — Yoko occupied a particular social position at Nevermore: the kind of cool that is recognized even by people who would not admit to recognizing it.

[APPEARANCE AND STYLE]
Yoko's visual identity was intentional and coherent: pastel-dyed hair in carefully maintained segments, dark eye makeup, and clothing that drew on Japanese street fashion — particularly the overlap between Harajuku aesthetic and gothic sensibility — to produce an effect that read as polished rather than assembled. Dark sunglasses, her concession to the vampire's standard relationship with bright light, became a signature rather than an accommodation.

[ABILITIES AND SPECIES]
As a vampire, Yoko possesses the standard attributes of her kind: heightened strength and reflexes, significantly extended lifespan, and photosensitivity managed through tinted eyewear. She experiences the typical garlic allergy shared by vampires and navigates daylight without fatal risk — discomfort, not danger.

[AFFILIATION AND SOCIAL ROLE]
Yoko was a member of the Nightshade Society, placing her among Nevermore's most influential students. Her membership reflected both her social standing and her discretion — Nightshade membership requires demonstrated reliability, and Yoko's measured personality suited the organization's requirements.

During the period when Wednesday Addams' friendship with Enid Sinclair became strained, Enid temporarily moved into Yoko's room — an arrangement that served as an informal refuge, as Yoko had the social grace to offer hospitality without requiring explanation.

[CURRENT STATUS]
Yoko does not appear in the second season of Wednesday. The circumstances of her departure from Nevermore are not addressed on-screen; she is simply absent, leaving behind a social impression that, as tends to be the case with students who leave quietly, is larger in retrospect than it seemed at the time.

Marilyn Thornhill was a normie botany teacher and dormitory supervisor at Nevermore Academy during Wednesday Addams' first year — and the primary antagonist of that year's events. She was later revealed to be Laurel Gates: the last surviving member of the Gates family, a devoted acolyte of Joseph Crackstone, and the architect of a plan to resurrect the long-dead pilgrim and complete his original mission of exterminating every outcast in Nevermore Academy.

[BACKGROUND AND IDENTITY]
Laurel Gates constructed the "Marilyn Thornhill" identity with considerable care. Her real name had been erased from public records years earlier, following her presumed death in circumstances she engineered herself. She held genuine botanical expertise, which made her cover both functional and nearly impenetrable. She applied for a faculty position at Nevermore by exploiting the academy's policy of allowing normie teachers — provided they received principal approval — and passed the screening that Larissa Weems conducted, a failure of intelligence that would ultimately cost Weems her life.

Her motivation was ideological and hereditary: raised in the Gates family tradition of anti-outcast fanaticism, she viewed Crackstone's original massacre as righteous action interrupted before completion. She spent years building toward a resurrection that would allow him to finish the work. Her position at Nevermore was not incidental to this plan — it was the plan.

[ROLE AT NEVERMORE]
As "Ms. Thornhill," she taught Botany and served as the dormitory supervisor for the girls' residential hall. She cultivated a persona of warm professionalism: encouraging to students, accessible to those in difficulty, and apparently sympathetic to the outcast community she was privately committed to destroying. This performance was sustained for an extended period and fooled nearly everyone.

Simultaneously, she identified Tyler Galpin as a dormant Hyde and spent months awakening and controlling him through a combination of chemical compounds and hypnosis, directing his attacks to weaken Nevermore's community and acquire the specific components needed for Crackstone's resurrection.

[UNMASKING AND DEFEAT]
Her true identity was uncovered by Wednesday Addams, who traced botanical evidence from the attack sites to Thornhill's specialized knowledge. When confronted, Laurel abandoned her cover entirely. She was ultimately incapacitated in the final confrontation by a swarm of bees directed by Eugene Ottinger — a fitting end given her botanical expertise — and subsequently arrested by law enforcement. Her legal proceedings following this are not shown.

[LEGACY]
Thornhill's infiltration of Nevermore is considered its most serious security failure in living memory, prompting significant changes to the faculty vetting process under Principal Barry Dort and a broader internal review of the academy's normie hiring policy.
