Xavier Thorpe is a psychic student who attended Nevermore Academy during Wednesday Addams' first year, notable both for his exceptional artistic ability and for the distinctive way his psychic power manifests: through his work. Xavier is a telekinetic animator — his sketches, paintings, and drawings, once completed, can be brought to life, the figures within them moving and acting under the influence of his visions and emotional state.

[POWERS AND ABILITIES]
Xavier's psychic classification is telekinetic-expressive — a comparatively rare variant in which psychic power channels through creative output rather than direct perception or manipulation. In practice, this means his artwork is not merely art: characters he sketches have walked off pages; animals he paints have emerged from canvas. The degree of animation and the accuracy of the resulting figures depend heavily on his emotional state. During periods of intense feeling — fear, obsession, grief — his creations become more vivid, more autonomous, and more difficult to control.

During the events of Wednesday's first year, his drawings repeatedly depicted the creature responsible for attacks in and around Jericho before the creature's identity was known. This was less vision than it appeared: Xavier had, without fully understanding it, captured something he had genuinely witnessed. This led to a period during which he was incorrectly suspected of involvement in the attacks.

[PERSONALITY AND RELATIONSHIPS]
Xavier is introspective and reserved, more likely to express complicated thoughts through his artwork than through direct conversation. He is perceptive — in the way that people who observe carefully rather than speak frequently tend to be — and carries a quiet frustration with being consistently misread by others. His initial romantic interest in Wednesday Addams developed into mutual respect and eventual strained reconciliation following the events that cleared his name.

His membership in the Nightshade Society reflects both his social standing — his father is the celebrity psychic Ansel Thorpe — and his genuine capabilities.

[CURRENT STATUS]
Xavier does not appear in the second season of Wednesday. His absence is explained by the new principal: following the events of his first year, Xavier's father removed him from Nevermore and enrolled him in a private academy in Switzerland. His reputation and the influence of his artwork remain present at Nevermore in his absence.

content:
Larissa Weems was the principal of Nevermore Academy for many years before her death during Wednesday Addams' first year at the school. A shapeshifter by species, a former Nevermore student by history, and a deeply pragmatic protector of the institution by vocation, she was one of the most formidable figures in the outcast world of her generation — and one of its more complicated ones.

[BACKGROUND]
Weems attended Nevermore as a student during the same era as Gomez and Morticia Addams, forming relationships with both that she maintained — in the particular way long-shared history is maintained — throughout her adult life. The dynamic between Weems and Morticia in particular carried layers that neither publicly explained, though Wednesday's arrival at the school reignited old tensions alongside whatever else existed between their families.

After graduating, Weems returned to Nevermore in a faculty capacity and eventually assumed the principal's role, a position she held with enough authority that most people stopped trying to remember who held it before her.

[ABILITIES]
As a shapeshifter, Weems could replicate the physical appearance and voice of any human individual she chose. She deployed this ability with exceptional discipline — it was not a trick she performed casually. The occasions on which she used it were deliberate and strategic, undertaken when the safety of the school or a specific student required something that her own face and title could not achieve.

[PHILOSOPHY AND LEADERSHIP]
Weems believed that Nevermore's function as a sanctuary was worth protecting through methods that would not survive public scrutiny. She concealed information she judged dangerous to share, made decisions unilaterally when she believed collective deliberation would produce worse outcomes, and maintained the school's reputation through calculated management of how it appeared to the outside world. These instincts served Nevermore well in many situations and created genuine blind spots in others.

She was not warm in the conventional sense. She was, to students who needed it, available — which is different and sometimes more useful.

[DEATH]
Weems was murdered by Marilyn Thornhill — Laurel Gates — who poisoned her with a nightshade-derived compound. She died before she could act on suspicions she had begun to develop about Thornhill's identity, and before she could warn Wednesday. She was found in the morning. Classes were not canceled. Weems, who had spent her career ensuring Nevermore's continuity, would likely have approved of the decision.
